text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The former head of the Swedish road authority Per Anders Ortendahl allegedly signed an unlawful agreement with Swedish automotive group AB Volvo and concrete maker Fardig Betong six years ago, according to the paper's own investigation. The deal meant the road authority performed research worth millions of crowns annually for the benefit of RST Sweden, an associated company set up by Ortendahl.
- A class society is re-emerging in Sweden, with increased gaps between different groups and the poor becoming more and more unhealthy, according to a government research group.

- Norwegian authorities refused to allow eight stowaways on a Swedish freight ship docking in a Norwegian harbour to leave the ship. The captain may be forced to continue his trip with the six Algerians, a Moroccan and a Palestinian aboard. The ship Nordon was on its way from North Africa to Karmoy in southwestern Norway when the stowaways were detected.
- The management of Swedish unions almost solely consists of men around 50 years of age with fairly high incomes, despite almost half of union members being women, a poll shows.

- Swedish telecoms group AB LM Ericsson is increasing its efforts on the digital mobile telecommunications standard Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA), recently submitting a tender for a broad-band system in Japan. Ericsson has favoured Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA), a competing system.

- The Maylasian government's investigation of an old contract between state-owned Malaysian telecoms company Telekom and Swedish telecoms group AB LM Ericsson reached new levels on Sunday when Malaysia's main opposition leader called for the government to reveal what minister is suspected in the deal.
- The former head of vehicle maker AB Volvo, Pehr Gyllenhammar, has been named as a candidate to replace Maria Leissner who had been expected to resign as head of the liberal Folk Party.

- Today's multi-millionaires are young computer experts. The founders of computer company Daydream, which was listed on the Stockholm bourse on Friday, now have shares worth 24 million crowns each after the stock price rocketed 600 percent.

- Last year Swedish banking group S-E-Banken, through its unit Enskilda Securities, increased its market share on share options on the OM securities and derivatives exchange with ten percentage points to 31 percent.

But trading with share related options on the OM exchange fell last year, despite share trading turnover reaching new record highs on the Stockholm bourse. Brokerages estimate that OM lost half the market to the non-standardised market as OM, bucking general trends, refused to lower its clearing fees.
